posts.excerpt: One-tap light and dark mode for any Framer site — flips the whole page, remembers the visitor's choice, and works with your existing Color Styles.
posts.html:
Smart Theme Switch – Add Light & Dark Mode to Any Framer Site

Smart Theme Switch is a Framer code component that adds a one-tap light and dark mode toggle to your site. It flips every page instantly, remembers each visitor's choice, and works with your existing Framer Color Styles automatically. No custom code, no duplicated styles, no flash of the wrong theme.


Get component

What Smart Theme Switch Does

Framer already lets you design light and dark variants of your Color Styles, but by default a visitor only ever sees the version that matches their device. There is no built-in way to give them a switch — and rolling your own means writing code that rewrites stylesheets, tracking state across pages, and hoping nothing breaks on export.

Smart Theme Switch handles all of it. Drop the component onto any page, point it at your brand colors, and it becomes a live control that flips your entire site between light and dark on a single tap. It reads the light and dark styles Framer already generates and re-applies the set the visitor chooses — so every background, text color, border, and surface repaints together, with zero manual wiring.

How It Works

When you use Color Styles in Framer, Framer compiles them into light and dark variants behind the scenes. Smart Theme Switch reads those variants and, when a visitor picks a theme, applies the matching set across the whole page — without ever modifying Framer's own stylesheets.

That approach keeps it safe and automatic. It works with the styles you already have, adds nothing to the page until a visitor actually interacts with it, and leaves your site behaving exactly like stock Framer for anyone who never touches the switch.


Features

Whole-Page Flip

One tap repaints the entire site. Backgrounds, text, borders, strokes, and every themed surface change together in a single click — not just the area around the toggle.

Remembers the Visitor's Choice

A visitor's selection is saved to their browser and restored on their next visit and on every other page of your site. Choose dark once and the site stays dark as they navigate and when they come back later.

Light, Dark, or Device

Set how the toggle starts:

  • Light — always open in light mode
  • Dark — always open in dark mode
  • Device — follow the visitor's system setting automatically, then let them override it

Style Every Part

Tune the switch to match your brand. Every part is a control:

  • Separate track and thumb colors for light and dark
  • Stroke width and color
  • Padding and corner sizing
  • Optional backdrop blur for glass-style tracks
  • Custom animation for the thumb, from a soft spring to an instant snap

Custom Icons

Show a sun and moon inside the thumb, or upload your own SVGs for each state with independent colors and size. Turn icons off entirely for a clean, minimal switch.

Built for Accessibility

The toggle is a proper switch, not just a styled div. It announces its label and on/off state to screen readers, is fully keyboard operable, and shows a customizable focus ring for keyboard users.

Multiple Toggles, One State

Place a switch in your header, your footer, and your mobile menu — they all stay in sync. Flipping any one of them updates the theme and every other toggle on the page at once.

Property Controls

Everything is editable from the Framer properties panel, no code required:

  • Default — Light, Dark, or Device
  • Label — the accessible name announced to screen readers
  • Track & Thumb colors — separate values for light and dark
  • Stroke — width and color
  • Padding — spacing around the thumb
  • Backdrop Blur — optional blur behind the track
  • Icons — show/hide, custom SVGs, colors, and size
  • Focus Ring — color and width
  • Animation — the thumb's transition

How to Add It to Your Site

  1. Install Smart Theme Switch from the Framer Marketplace
  2. Open your Framer project and drag the component onto your header or nav
  3. Set your light and dark track, thumb, and stroke colors to match your brand
  4. Choose how it starts — Light, Dark, or Device
  5. Publish your site
  6. The live flip runs on your published and preview links — tap it to test

Pricing

Smart Theme Switch is free. Install it from the Framer Marketplace and add unlimited toggles to your project — no license key, no usage limits.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need to set anything up for it to work?

No. If you use Framer Color Styles with light and dark values, the toggle works automatically. Just drop it in and pick your colors.

Will it work with my existing dark mode styles?

Yes. It reads the light and dark variants Framer already generates from your Color Styles, so it matches your existing design with no extra configuration.

Does the choice persist across pages and visits?

Yes. A visitor's selection is stored in their browser, kept as they move between pages, and restored the next time they return.

Can visitors follow their device theme automatically?

Yes. Set the default to Device and the site opens in whatever theme the visitor's system uses, while still letting them override it with the switch.

Will it slow down my site or affect SEO?

No. The component stays completely inert until a visitor interacts with it and never rewrites Framer's own stylesheets, so pages that are never toggled behave exactly like stock Framer.

Why doesn't the switch animate on the Framer canvas?

On the canvas and during export it shows a clean static preview by design. The live flip runs on your published and preview links, not inside the editor.

Can I use my own icons?

Yes. Upload custom SVGs for the light and dark states, set their colors and size, or turn icons off for a minimal look.

StyleSync - Import Design Tokens & Styles into Framer

StyleSync is a Framer plugin that extracts actively-used styles from your Figma files, design token files, and websites, and imports them directly into Framer as native color and text styles. No manual copying, no missed tokens, no mismatched values.

What StyleSync Does

Every design workflow involves moving styles between tools. Designers maintain color palettes and typography in Figma, developers define tokens in CSS or JSON, and production sites carry their own computed styles. Getting those values into Framer accurately and quickly is tedious work done manually.

StyleSync automates that transfer. It reads your styles from wherever they live, shows you a preview with full control over what gets imported, and injects only the styles you select directly into your Framer project as native color styles and text styles, accessible from any element in the canvas.

Import Methods

StyleSync supports three distinct import methods, each designed for a different point in your workflow.

Figma File Import

Paste any Figma file URL and StyleSync scans the entire document for actively-used styles. Rather than pulling every style defined in the file including unused library styles, StyleSync walks the document tree and extracts only the styles that are actually applied to elements. This keeps your Framer style panel clean and relevant.

Supported:

  • Fill colors and solid color styles
  • Typography styles including font family, size, weight, line height, and letter spacing
  • Both local styles and shared library styles in use

To use Figma import you will need a Figma Personal Access Token. You can generate one in Figma under Settings → Security → Personal access tokens. Name it anything, copy it, and paste it once into StyleSync. It is stored locally and never transmitted to any third party.

Upload File

If your team works with design tokens in code, upload your token file directly. StyleSync parses the file client-side and extracts all color and typography values.

Supported formats:

  • CSS files — extracts custom properties from :root, resolves var() references, handles clamp() values
  • JSON files — supports Tokens Studio format, Figma Variables export, and W3C Design Tokens specification

Drag and drop your file or click to browse. StyleSync auto-detects the format and parses it immediately.

Paste Code

Skip the file entirely and paste CSS or JSON directly into the plugin. Useful for copying styles from a codebase, a Storybook, or a design system documentation site. StyleSync auto-detects whether the pasted content is CSS or JSON and processes it accordingly.

Website URL

Enter any public website URL and StyleSync extracts the CSS custom properties and computed color and typography values from the live site. Useful for matching an existing brand's styles or importing from a live design system documentation site.

Style Preview and Selection

Before anything is imported you see a full preview of every extracted style. Each style shows its name, value, and a visual swatch for colors or a type sample for text styles.

You can:

  • Select individual styles using checkboxes
  • Use Select All / Deselect All
  • Review exactly what will be imported before committing

Only the styles you select are imported. Nothing is written to your Framer project until you confirm.

What Gets Created in Framer

StyleSync creates native Framer styles, not overrides or custom properties. After import:

  • Color styles appear in your Framer color panel, available from any fill, stroke, or background picker
  • Text styles appear in your Framer text styles panel, applicable to any text element

Styles are named exactly as they appear in the source file, preserving your naming conventions and token hierarchy.

Pricing

StyleSync is free to start with a usage limit on the free tier.

Yearly$49/yearUnlimited (save 54%)
Lifetime$89 one-timeUnlimited forever

Usage is tracked server-side, tied to your Framer account. Upgrading to Pro unlocks unlimited imports across all three import methods.

How to Get Started

  1. Install StyleSync from the Framer Marketplace
  2. Open any Framer project
  3. Go to Plugins → StyleSync
  4. Choose your import method
  5. Preview and select your styles
  6. Click Import

How to Get a Figma Access Token

For Figma file imports StyleSync requires a Personal Access Token. Here is how to generate one:

  1. Open Figma and click your avatar in the top left
  2. Go to Settings
  3. Scroll to Security
  4. Under Personal access tokens click Generate new token
  5. Give it a name like "StyleSync"
  6. Copy the token and paste it into StyleSync

The token is stored locally in your browser and is only used to read your Figma file. It is never sent to Visuvate servers.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does StyleSync import all styles in a Figma file?

No. StyleSync only extracts styles that are actively applied to elements in your file. Unused library styles are ignored, keeping your import clean.

Can I use StyleSync without a Figma account?

Yes. The Upload File and Website URL methods work without any Figma connection.

What happens to my Figma token?

Your token is stored locally in your browser only. It is used exclusively to read file data from Figma's API and is never transmitted to Visuvate.

Does importing overwrite existing Framer styles?

No. StyleSync creates new styles. If a style with the same name already exists in Framer it will be added alongside it, not replaced.

I upgraded my plan. How do I activate Pro?

After purchasing you will receive a license key by email. Open StyleSync, click the gear icon, go to Account, and enter your license key.

posts.title: Smart Animated Counters in Wix Studio
posts.excerpt: Learn how to add smart animated number counters to your Wix Studio site. This step-by-step guide provides a copy-and-paste Velo code snippet that automatically handles complex formats, such as 10k, $500, or 98% satisfaction.
posts.html:
How to Add a Smart Counter in Wix Studio (The Animated Way)

Nothing grabs attention on a portfolio or landing page quite like animated statistics. Whether it’s "10k+ Views" or "100% Satisfaction," watching numbers count up creates a sense of momentum.

If you are looking for the perfect Counter in Wix Studio, you might have realized that standard text elements don't animate by default. In this tutorial, I’m sharing a robust Velo (JavaScript) snippet that I use on my projects. It’s "smart" because it automatically handles suffixes (k, M, B), decimals, and symbols (%) without you needing to write extra code for each text box.

The Outcome

By the end of this guide, you will have text elements that automatically count up from 0 when the user scrolls them into view, acting as a fully dynamic Counter in Wix Studio.

Step 1: Open the Code Panel

You don't need to install anything complex to get this working.

  1. In the Wix Studio Editor, look at the left sidebar.
  2. Click the { } (Code) icon.
  3. A panel will slide up at the bottom of your screen. This is where we will paste the code.

Step 2: Prepare Your Text Elements

The code needs to know which text elements to animate. To create a specific Counter in Wix Studio, we use a specific ID.

  1. Add a Text Element to your canvas.

  2. Type in your final number (e.g., 1500, 98%, $10k).

    • Note: You can style the font, size, and color however you like.
  3. Select the text element.
  4. Look at the bottom right of your screen (next to the code editor) to find the Properties & Events panel.
  5. Find the ID field.

  6. Change the ID to start with num.

    • Examples: numCounter1, numStats, numRevenue.

The code specifically looks for IDs starting with "num" and ignores everything else.

⚠️ Important Limitation: This code is designed for static text elements only. It will not work for text elements inside a Repeater (connected to the CMS). Repeaters require a different coding approach using onItemReady.

Step 3: The Code

Copy the code below and paste it directly into the panel at the bottom of your screen. (Note: If you see existing code like $w.onReady..., you can delete it and replace it with this complete snippet.)

JavaScript

$w.onReady(() => {
  // CONFIGURATION: Animation Duration in milliseconds
  const DURATION = 1500;

  // 1. Find and Initialize all "num" elements
  $w('Text').forEach(el => {
    if (!el.id || !el.id.toLowerCase().startsWith('num')) return;
    initCounter(el);
  });

  // 2. The Core Counter Function
  function initCounter(el) {
    const original = (el.text || '').toString();
    // Regex to find numbers, decimals, commas, and suffixes (k, M, B)
    const matches = [...original.matchAll(/(\d[\d,]*(?:\.\d+)?(?:\s*[kKmMbB])?)([%\+]?)/g)];
    if (!matches.length) return;

    let template = original;
    matches.forEach((m, i) => {
      template = template.replace(m[0], `{{n${i}}}`);
    });

    const tokens = matches.map(m => {
      const rawNum = m[1].replace(/\s+/g, '');
      const trail = m[2] || '';
      return parseTokenPreserveShort(rawNum, trail);
    });

    const zeroState = () => tokens.map(t => formatDisplayValue(0, t));
    const finalState = () => tokens.map(t => formatDisplayValue(t.isShort ? t.shortValue : t.fullValue, t));

    // Reset text to 0 initially
    el.text = buildTextFromTemplate(template, zeroState(), tokens.map(t => t.trail));

    let started = false;

    // Animation Loop
    function animate() {
      if (started) return;
      started = true;
      const startTime = performance.now();

      function step(now) {
        const t = Math.min((now - startTime) / DURATION, 1);
        // Easing function (Cubic Ease Out) for smooth effect
        const eased = 1 - Math.pow(1 - t, 3);

        const current = tokens.map(tok => {
          const val = tok.isShort ? tok.shortValue * eased : tok.fullValue * eased;
          return formatDisplayValue(val, tok);
        });

        el.text = buildTextFromTemplate(template, current, tokens.map(t => t.trail));

        if (t < 1) {
          requestAnimationFrame(step);
        } else {
          el.text = buildTextFromTemplate(template, finalState(), tokens.map(t => t.trail));
        }
      }
      requestAnimationFrame(step);
    }

    // Trigger animation when element enters viewport
    el.onViewportEnter(animate);
    
    // Optional: Reset when leaving viewport so it plays again
    el.onViewportLeave(() => {
      started = false;
      el.text = buildTextFromTemplate(template, zeroState(), tokens.map(t => t.trail));
    });
  }
});

/* ================= HELPERS (Paste these outside onReady) ================= */

function parseTokenPreserveShort(rawNum, trail) {
  // UPDATED: Do not force lowercase on the whole string immediately
  // Regex now looks for uppercase or lowercase suffixes: [kKmMbB]
  const shortMatch = rawNum.match(/^([\d.,]+)([kKmMbB])$/);

  if (shortMatch) {
    const num = parseFloat(shortMatch[1].replace(/,/g, ''));
    const originalSuffix = shortMatch[2]; // "M" or "m"
    const lowerSuffix = originalSuffix.toLowerCase(); // used for math only
    
    const multiplier = lowerSuffix === 'k' ? 1e3 : lowerSuffix === 'm' ? 1e6 : 1e9;
    const decimals = (shortMatch[1].split('.')[1] || '').length;

    return {
      isShort: true,
      suffix: originalSuffix, // Preserves the original Case (e.g. "M")
      shortValue: num,
      fullValue: num * multiplier,
      decimals,
      hasSeparator: /,/.test(rawNum),
      trail
    };
  }

  const numeric = parseFloat(rawNum.replace(/,/g, ''));
  const decimals = (rawNum.split('.')[1] || '').length;

  return {
    isShort: false,
    suffix: '',
    shortValue: null,
    fullValue: isFinite(numeric) ? numeric : 0,
    decimals,
    hasSeparator: /,/.test(rawNum),
    trail
  };
}

function formatDisplayValue(value, tok) {
  const rounded = tok.decimals === 0 ? Math.round(value) : roundToDecimals(value, tok.decimals);
  if (tok.isShort) {
    return tok.decimals === 0 
      ? `${rounded}${tok.suffix}` 
      : `${rounded.toFixed(tok.decimals)}${tok.suffix}`;
  }
  if (tok.hasSeparator) {
    return Number(rounded).toLocaleString(undefined, {
      minimumFractionDigits: tok.decimals,
      maximumFractionDigits: tok.decimals
    });
  }
  return String(rounded);
}

function buildTextFromTemplate(template, values, trails) {
  let text = template;
  values.forEach((v, i) => { text = text.replace(`{{n${i}}}`, v + (trails[i] || '')); });
  return text;
}

function roundToDecimals(num, dec) {
  const m = Math.pow(10, dec);
  return Math.round((num + Number.EPSILON) * m) / m;
}

Understanding the Code (What you can change)

You don't need to be a coding expert to tweak this Counter in Wix Studio. Here is the one value you might want to adjust:

The Animation Speed At the very top of the code, find this line: const DURATION = 1500;

posts.html:
Adding smooth scrolling to your Wix website enhances user experience by creating a fluid and polished transition between scroll actions.

In this guide, we will implement smooth scrolling using Lenis, a lightweight JavaScript library for smooth page scrolling.

Requirements

  • A Wix Premium Plan (Custom code functionality is only available in premium plans).

Smooth Scroll in a Wix Website Guide

Step 1: Adding the Custom Code

To enable smooth scrolling, we will use Lenis.js. Below is the custom code you need to add to your Wix website:

<script src="https://unpkg.com/@studio-freight/lenis@1.0.42/dist/lenis.min.js"></script>

<style>

/* Ensure the page height is correctly set for Lenis */

html.lenis, html.lenis body {

height: auto;

}

/* Override default scroll behavior */

.lenis.lenis-smooth {

scroll-behavior: auto !important;

}

/* Prevent scrolling when necessary */

.lenis.lenis-stopped {

overflow: hidden;

}

</style>

<script>

// Initialize Lenis with smooth scrolling configuration

const lenis = new Lenis({

lerp: 0.1, // Damping effect for smoothness

wheelMultiplier: 0.7, // Adjust scroll speed

gestureOrientation: 'vertical', // Enable vertical scrolling

normalizeWheel: false, // Preserve native wheel behavior

smoothTouch: false // Disable smooth scrolling for touch devices

});

// Animation frame loop to keep Lenis active

function raf(time) {

lenis.raf(time);

requestAnimationFrame(raf);

}

requestAnimationFrame(raf);

</script>

Step 2: Implementing the Code in Wix Studio

Follow these steps to add the custom code to your Wix website:

  1. Go to your Wix Studio dashboard.
  2. On the bottom-left, click Settings.
  3. In Settings, search or scroll down to find Custom Code.
  4. Click Add Custom Code.

  5. In the pop-up panel:

    • Paste the custom code in the "Paste the code snippet here:" box.
    • Give it a recognizable name like "Smooth Scroll".
    • Apply the code to all pages.
    • Set the placement to Head.
  6. Click Apply.

Step 3: Testing the Smooth Scroll Effect

  • Refresh your published website to activate the smooth scrolling effect.
  • Scroll up and down to experience the fluid transition.
  • If you want to adjust the smoothness, modify the lerp and wheelMultiplier values in the script.

Credits

  • Lenis.js developed by Studio Freight

Conclusion

Adding smooth scrolling to a Wix website significantly improves the user experience, giving it a professional touch. Following this guide, you can effortlessly integrate Lenis.js and achieve a seamless scrolling effect on your Wix site.

It is a small polish detail, and exactly the kind of thing our Motion & Interaction Design service builds into client sites by default.

posts.html:
Learn how to create a stunning editable vector text effect using the Appearance and Graphic Styles panels in Adobe Illustrator.

This step-by-step tutorial will show you how to design a spider web text effect that can be reused as a template for any text!

Introduction

Adobe Illustrator is a powerful tool for creating editable vector text effects that can be reused across multiple projects. In this tutorial, I’ll show you how to make a spider web text effect using the Appearance and Graphic Styles panels. This effect is fully editable, meaning you can apply it to any text with just one click! Whether you’re a beginner or an experienced designer, this guide will help you master Illustrator’s advanced features.

What You’ll Need

  • Adobe Illustrator (any recent version).
  • Basic knowledge of Illustrator tools (Type Tool, Appearance Panel, etc.).

Editable vector text effect

Step 1: Set Up Your Text

  1. Open Adobe Illustrator and create a new document.
  2. Select the Type Tool (T) and type your text (e.g., “WEB”).
  3. Set the text size to 400px and use a bold font for better visibility.
  4. Remove the fill colour from the text using the left tool panel.

Step 2: Enable the Appearance Panel

  1. Go to the Window menu and enable the Appearance Panel.
  2. With your text selected, you’ll see “Type” listed in the Appearance Panel.

Step 3: Add a Stroke and Apply the Roughen Effect

  1. In the Appearance Panel, click the Stroke icon at the bottom to add a stroke to your text.
  2. With the stroke selected, click the Effects Menu (fx) and choose: Distort & Transform > Roughen.

  3. In the Roughen settings:

    • Set Size to 100% (Absolute).
    • Set Detail to 5/in.
    • Select Points > Corner.
    • Click OK.

Step 4: Duplicate and Customize Strokes

  1. In the Appearance Panel, click the Plus Icon at the bottom to duplicate the stroke. Create a total of 6 strokes.

  2. Adjust the stroke sizes from top to bottom:

    • 1pt, 1pt, 0.75pt, 0.50pt, 0.25pt, 0.1pt.

  3. Modify the Roughen effect size for each stroke:

    • 10px, 20px, 40px, 60px, 80px, 100px.

This creates a layered, spider web-like effect on your text.

Step 5: Save the Effect as a Graphic Style

  1. Open the Graphic Styles Panel (Window > Graphic Styles).
  2. With your text selected, drag it into the Graphic Styles Panel. This saves the editable vector text effect in a reusable style.

  3. To apply the effect to new text:

    • Type your desired text.
    • Select the text and click the saved style in the Graphic Styles Panel.

Why Use Graphic Styles for Text Effects?

  • Reusability: Apply the same effect to multiple texts instantly.
  • Editable: Modify the original style, and all applied texts will update automatically.
  • Consistency: Maintain a uniform design across your projects.

Pro Tips for Customizing Your Text Effect

  • Experiment with different stroke colours for a unique look.
  • Adjust the Roughen effect settings to create variations (e.g., smoother or sharper edges).
  • Combine this effect with other Illustrator tools (e.g., gradients, brushes) for more complex designs.

Conclusion

Creating an editable vector text effect in Adobe Illustrator is a game-changer for designers. With the Appearance and Graphic Styles panels, you can design stunning effects like the spider web text effect and reuse them effortlessly. Try this tutorial and elevate your design projects today!

Reusable, consistent visual assets like this are exactly what our Consistent Identity service builds for a brand across every touchpoint.

posts.html:
How to Add a Stylish Wix Studio Preloader to Your Website (Step-by-Step Guide)

Want to make your website more engaging with a sleek preloader animation? In this guide, I’ll show you how to implement a custom preloader using Wix’s built-in tools and a bit of code. Let’s get started!

What You’ll Need

  • A Wix website.
  • A loopable animation or video (you can use Wix’s library or upload your own).
  • Basic understanding of Wix’s editor.

Wix Studio Preloader Guide

Step 1: Create the Preloader Container

  1. Open your Wix editor and go to the page where you want to add the preloader.
  2. Add a Container element to your page.
  3. Resize the container to fit the entire screen.
  4. Rename the container’s ID to #PreLoader (this is important for the code to work).
  5. Pin the container:
  6. Click on the container.
  7. Go to the Position menu.
  8. Select Pinned to Page.

Step 2: Add a Loop Animation

  1. Inside the #PreLoader container, add a Video element.
  2. Choose a loopable animation:
  3. Use Wix’s built-in video library.
  4. Or upload your transparent video (e.g., a progress bar or logo animation).
  5. Adjust the video settings to loop seamlessly.

Step 3: Add the Preloader Code

  1. Go to the Page Code tab in your Wix editor.
  2. Paste the following code:

    // Preloader code
    $w.onReady(() => {
    $w('#header').hide(); // Hide header
    waitForLoading();
    });

    export function button_onClick() {
    $w('#PreLoader').show();
    waitForLoading();
    }

    function waitForLoading() {
    setTimeout(() => {
    $w('#PreLoader').collapse(); // Hide the preloader
    $w('#header').show('fade'); // Show header
    }, 3500); // Wait for miliseconds
    }

Step 4: Customize the Code

  • Change the duration: Adjust the 3500 value in the setTimeout function to match your video length or desired loading time.
  • Hide additional elements: If you want to hide more elements (e.g., footer, buttons), duplicate the $w('#header').hide(); line and replace #header with the ID of the element you want to hide.

Pro Tips

  • Use a transparent video for a modern look, or match the preloader container’s background colour to your video.
  • For a progress bar animation, ensure the video length and code duration are perfectly synced.
  • Experiment with different animations to match your website’s vibe.

Why Add a Preloader?

A preloader isn’t just visually appealing—it also improves user experience by giving visitors something to look at while your page loads. Plus, it’s a great way to showcase your creativity!

Final Thoughts

Adding a Wix Studio Preloader to your website is a simple yet effective way to elevate its design. With this guide, you can implement it in just a few steps. Try it out and let me know how it goes!

This kind of loading polish is one of the details our Motion & Interaction Design service handles on client builds.

Photo-led layouts, a hero that fits a laptop screen, and dropdown menus with treatment previews keep navigation light without hiding anything.

Built as a custom WordPress theme with editable Elementor widgets, Aveline lets the practice update treatments, specialists, journal articles, and bookings without touching the design, while a live slot picker and written estimate flow keep the patient journey simple across every device.

projects.title: Parley
projects.metaTitle: Parley — Website Design Case Study | Visuvate
projects.overview: Parley is a website for a customer support, trust and safety and back-office company, built around a reply with a name, four studios that hand over the queue, published rates and a team estimator.
projects.brief: A BPO that runs customer support, trust and safety and back office for consumer brands wanted a site that sounds like the people it hires. Buyers needed to see how a team is built, where it sits, what it costs and who answers, without a long sales form in the way.
projects.approach: Every reply has a name. The hero pairs a customer message with the agent who answers it, in a serif for the customer and a wide grotesk for the reply, over portraits of the four studios. Services, a follow-the-sun view, the six-week process, a weekly report, published rates and a team estimator follow.
projects.outcome: A buyer can see the three kinds of work, the four studios and how the queue is handed over, read a real weekly report, price a team and ask for a plan in a few minutes. The pages stay light and quick for a visitor on any device.
projects.about:
Parley is a complete website for a business process outsourcing company founded in Cebu in 2012, with about 1,400 people in Bogotá, Cebu, Cape Town and Lisbon. It is designed to make a buyer’s first look easy: what each team does, where it works, how it is run and what it costs.

The site includes Home, Services with customer support, trust and safety and back office, How we work, Rates, Plan a team, Locations, Clients with three case studies and Careers, plus Privacy, Terms and 404 pages.

The visual direction is calm and editorial: a paper page, ink and one ultramarine accent, a light italic serif for the customer and Mona Sans for the reply, daylight photography of real teams, square panels and no shadows. Headlines resolve line by line, photographs reveal behind a curtain and the studios hand the queue over as the clock turns.

Built as a fast static site in Astro with plain TypeScript, GSAP and Lenis, Parley respects reduced-motion settings and works on a phone. The team estimator, plan-a-team form and careers filters are built in.

projects.title: Ellery Kowal
projects.metaTitle: Ellery Kowal — Website Design Case Study | Visuvate
projects.overview: Ellery Kowal is a website for a 41-lawyer business law firm on LaSalle Street in Chicago, built around the questions a general counsel asks first: who will lead the matter, how it is billed and what the firm has achieved. A statue hero, working client tools and a results ledger replace the usual brochure.
projects.brief: A Chicago business law firm with 41 lawyers needed a website that earns a general counsel’s trust before the first call: who leads a matter, how it is billed, what past results look like, and a conflict check that does not feel like a form wall. It had to read as established and current, not as another dark, shouting law site.
projects.approach: We built the site around one idea, that every word is evidence. A bronze statue and a slow court-seal ring open a cream page set in Gambetta and General Sans, with working tools for booking a strategy call and finding a fixed fee, then a results ledger, partner portraits and a conflict-check letter.
projects.outcome: A prospective client can see the six practices and their fee models, meet the partner who would lead the work, read results without client names, and start a conflict check in a few minutes. Seven pages and three articles stay quick on a phone.
projects.about:
Ellery Kowal is a complete website for a Chicago business law firm founded in 2011, with six practices from trials and disputes to corporate and M&A, employment, investigations, real estate and IP. It is designed to make a first conversation easy: a partner to call, a fee model for every practice and a conflict check that takes minutes.

The site includes Home, Practices with fee models and results, People with seven partners and a directory of all 41 lawyers, Matters with a filterable results ledger, the Firm, Insights with three articles and Contact with a live map, plus Privacy and Disclaimer pages.

The visual direction is warm and professional: a cream page, ink and one bronze accent, Gambetta for headings and General Sans for text, bright daylight photography, square hairline panels instead of shadows and a bronze statue with a rotating court-seal ring in the hero. Every accordion, filter and menu animates both ways.

Built as a fast static site in Astro with plain TypeScript, Ellery Kowal loads quickly on a phone, keeps motion calm and respects reduced-motion settings. The conflict-check, strategy-call and fee-finder tools, and the OpenFreeMap-based contact map, are built in.

projects.title: Photofolio
projects.metaTitle: Photofolio — Website Design Case Study | Visuvate
projects.overview: Photofolio is a photography portfolio website for a portrait, family, event and wedding photographer. The first screen is a contact sheet you can drag, and every page keeps the photographs as the interface.
projects.brief: A photographer needed a site where the interface disappears. Photography sites fail in two directions: chrome that competes with the images, or minimalism so severe the work floats without context. The brief: photographs first, with just enough structure that a visitor can still find a service, a price and a way to book.
projects.approach: We built a dark, quiet frame around the work. The home page opens on a contact sheet you can drag, then moves through a pinned statement, a gallery you move through sideways, four services and a film strip of how a shoot works. Every project is one real session, so a page never mixes light or people. Built with Astro, GSAP and Lenis.
projects.outcome: The site behaves like a well-hung exhibition: the eye moves from image to image with nothing pulling at its sleeve. Services show a clear price and a one-page plan, projects open into a gallery that respects each photograph's shape, and the journal gives the practice a voice between commissions.
projects.about:
Photofolio is a complete website for a portrait, family, event and wedding photographer, built with Astro and designed to put the photographs first. A dark, calm layout keeps the colour in the images, and nothing decorative competes with them.

The home page opens on a contact sheet you can drag, then moves through a pinned statement that changes rooms as you scroll, a gallery you move through sideways, four services with prices, a film strip showing how a shoot works, client notes and the journal.

Each of the thirteen projects is a single session, shown in a gallery that respects the shape of every photograph and opens into a lightbox. Services, About, Journal and Contact share one type system: Host Grotesk for headlines and Geist Mono for captions.

The site is fully responsive and built from structured content, so sessions, services and journal notes can be added without touching the layout.

projects.title: Tubwell
projects.metaTitle: Tubwell — Website Design Case Study | Visuvate
projects.overview: Tubwell is a dog and cat grooming website with a shop and self-wash tubs, built to make a first booking feel friendly. Clear prices, a groom card for every pet and a text-when-ready promise replace the usual vague price list.
projects.brief: A neighbourhood groomer needed a website that answers the questions owners are nervous about before booking: what it costs for my dog, how the pet is dried, and who is holding the scissors. Most grooming sites hide prices behind stock photos, so the brief was a cheerful, honest site that shows both.
projects.approach: We built Tubwell around price tags, a groom card and house rules. Prices hang on tags by dog size, every pet gets a card with its coat, cut and notes, and a soft pastel palette with hand-lettered touches keeps the tone playful. It runs on WordPress with Elementor, so the team can edit it.
projects.outcome: The site now reads like the shop it represents: owners can price a groom, meet the regulars, see how pets are dried and book from the same page. The shop, self-wash tubs and studio each have their place, and everything stays editable so prices and products can change without a designer.
projects.about:
Tubwell is a complete website for a dog and cat grooming studio with a self-wash room and a small pickup shop. It was designed to make a first booking feel easy, with prices by dog size, a card for every regular and plain rules about how pets are handled.

The site includes Home, Grooming with the full price list, a booking request page, the Shop with thirteen products, a Studio page with the house rules and directions, and Privacy and Terms pages. Every price tag, groom card and product is its own editable item.

The visual direction uses soft lilac, peach and mint panels with a blue accent, Bricolage headlines and a hand-lettered note face. Pets peek over the service cards, price tags hang on a line and a groom card fans out like a real index card, so the page feels like the counter of a friendly shop.

Built on WordPress with Elementor, Tubwell keeps sections, layouts and content editable, with custom widgets only for the interactive parts such as the price picker, groom cards and bag drawer. Booking requests are saved inside WordPress.

projects.title: Tigre-Tigre
projects.metaTitle: Tigre-Tigre — Website Design Case Study | Visuvate
projects.overview: Tigre Tigre is a bold, visually rich restaurant website designed to showcase an authentic dining experience. The design combines striking photography, dark tones, and cultural typography to reflect the restaurant’s lively atmosphere and refined menu presentation.
projects.brief: A restaurant with genuine character needed a website that tasted like the room: bold, warm, and unmistakably itself. Menus, hours, and reservations had to be effortless to find — but wrapped in an experience that makes the booking feel like it has already begun.
projects.approach: We built the site around the photography — saturated dishes against dark, atmospheric grounds — and let cultural typography carry the brand’s voice. Reservations are integrated natively so a table is two taps from the hero, and motion is kept to slow, appetite-adjacent reveals rather than spectacle.
projects.outcome: The site now does what a good maître d’ does: sets the mood and removes friction in the same gesture. Diners arrive already sold on the atmosphere, the menu reads as a promise rather than a list, and booking a table takes less time than choosing a starter.
projects.about:
Tigre Tigre is a restaurant website designed to capture the authentic character of a modern dining and sake experience. The layout merges elegance with energy — using deep color palettes, textured backgrounds, and full-width imagery that highlight both the cuisine and ambiance of the restaurant.

The hero section immediately immerses visitors in the restaurant’s atmosphere with high-quality visuals and clear branding. The menu structure is presented in a clean, sectioned layout, dividing offerings such as starters, rolls, ramen, cocktails, and desserts for effortless browsing. Each category is paired with vibrant food photography to create an engaging and appetite-driven experience.

The visual hierarchy emphasizes both readability and mood, balancing bold headers with minimalist typography to reflect the sophistication of the venue. The footer section completes the journey with reservation details, contact links, and a social media gallery that enhances user interaction and brand connection.

Developed in Wix Studio, the design prioritizes responsiveness and smooth navigation across devices, ensuring every visitor can explore the restaurant’s offerings seamlessly. The result is a digital dining experience that mirrors the warmth, taste, and cultural depth of Tigre Tigre itself.

projects.title: Halden Roofing
projects.metaTitle: Halden Roofing — Website Design Case Study | Visuvate
projects.overview: Halden Roofing is a residential roofing website built to make a big, unfamiliar purchase feel simple. Photo inspection reports, fixed written prices, a live cost estimator and a clear booking path turn a roof replacement into a process homeowners can follow.
projects.brief: A family-run roofing company needed a website that earns trust before the first site visit. Homeowners rarely know what a roof should cost or what the work involves, so the site had to explain the process plainly, show real finished roofs and make booking an inspection easy.
projects.approach: We built the site around the paperwork homeowners actually receive: an inspection report, a written scope, a daily build log and a warranty. An asphalt and felt-paper palette with a hi-vis accent, Manrope type, a materials library and a cost estimator keep every page practical.
projects.outcome: The site now works like a well-run job: services, materials and projects are explained in plain terms, costs can be estimated before a call, and booking an inspection takes a minute. The pages share one system, so new projects and articles slot in cleanly.
projects.about:
Halden Roofing is a complete website for a residential roofing company, designed to take the guesswork out of replacing or repairing a roof. The project focuses on transparency, with fixed written prices, photo inspection reports and a clear path from first question to booked inspection.

The site includes Home, six service pages covering replacement, repairs, storm damage, inspections, gutters and ventilation, a materials library with a comparison table, a projects index with detailed case studies, About, a storm damage guide, a full cost estimator, a roofing journal and a contact page with inspection booking.

The visual direction pairs an asphalt ink and felt-paper palette with a hi-vis lime accent taken from the crew’s shirts, set in Manrope with generous spacing. A giant wordmark hero, job-sheet details on project cards and hairline lists keep the site practical and calm rather than salesy.

Built as a fast static site with smooth scrolling, roof-pitch image transitions and reduced-motion support, Halden stays quick and accessible on every device, and its shared page system makes new services, projects and articles easy to add.

projects.title: Horizone
projects.metaTitle: Horizone — Car Rental Website Case Study | Visuvate
projects.overview: Horizone is a car-rental booking site designed and built end to end — a full-screen hero with the search bar, a filterable fleet of 26 cars, car pages with live pricing, checkout and an account area, so a visitor goes from idea to confirmed trip on one site.
projects.brief: Car-rental sites bury the real price under fees and filters. Horizone needed to feel calm and trustworthy, and to let a visitor search, compare and reserve a car without ever losing track of the total.
projects.approach: We built the whole journey, not a landing page: a full-screen search hero, a filterable fleet, a car page with a live price panel, then checkout and confirmation, all in one consistent system of light and type.
projects.outcome: The site now behaves like a product. Visitors reach a price they trust in a few taps, the fleet looks consistent car to car, and each of the thirteen pages feels like part of one booking experience.
projects.about:
Horizone is a car-rental concept built as a complete booking product rather than a single landing page. A visitor searches a city and dates, compares a fleet of 26 cars, reserves one and lands on a confirmation, all on one site.

The site runs to thirteen pages: a home page with a full-screen hero and booking bar, a filterable fleet, a car page with a gallery and live price panel, checkout, confirmation, an account area, locations across 14 cities, deals, help, an about page and legal. Each one is designed to feel like part of the same journey.

Every car is shown in the same soft studio light so the fleet reads as one collection. A strict radius ladder keeps cards, panels and buttons consistent, and prices show fees and protection up front, so the total never changes at the last step.

Motion stays quiet and purposeful: gentle entrances, a sliding pill in the navigation and swipe rows on phones. The whole site is hand-built, fast, accessible and clear at every screen size.

projects.title: Forma
projects.metaTitle: Forma — Website Design Case Study | Visuvate
projects.overview: Forma is a SaaS workspace concept designed and built end to end — from the marketing home through Features, Pricing, Integrations, and a working sign-up flow — so a visitor moves through the same site a real product launch would ship, rather than a single page standing in for one.
projects.brief: A SaaS marketing site is judged on completeness, not just its hero — a buyer wants to see pricing, integrations, and security posture before they trust a product with their team's data, and most landing-page demos stop at the homepage.
projects.approach: Forma was built as twelve full pages rather than one, sharing a single dashboard mockup as the visual through-line. Dark and light themes were designed natively side by side, never one simply inverted from the other.
projects.outcome: The result reads as a shipped product rather than a mockup: a visitor moves from the headline through features and pricing into a real sign-up flow, landing on a dashboard preview that matches what was promised.
projects.about:
Forma is a SaaS workspace concept, built to prove that a marketing site can carry the full weight of a real product launch rather than a single hero section and a signup button — the studio's own answer to what a genuinely complete launch page looks like.

Twelve pages carry the story end to end: a marketing home, Features, Solutions by team, a public Integrations directory, three-tier Pricing, a Changelog that reads like a real one, and Security and legal pages that make the product feel shipped.

The interface runs natively in both a dark and a light theme rather than one inverted from the other, with a purple gradient and the same card language carried consistently from the hero through the pricing table to the dashboard mockups.

An animated product dashboard — task counts, a focus-time chart, a due-today list — stands in for the real app throughout the site, so a visitor evaluates something concrete rather than a single static screenshot on the homepage.

projects.title: Alvara House
projects.metaTitle: Alvara House — Website Design Case Study | Visuvate
projects.overview: A sixteen-page property site built from scratch in Next.js, with a complete light and dark treatment. It covers a property collection, individual listings, neighbourhood guides, partner profiles, a journal and the enquiry flow — all sharing one editorial type system.

shots.title: Alvara House homepage, the agency wordmark set over a coastal house at dusk
The property collection, each listing credited to its architect
Services page setting out the four practices the agency runs
Neighbourhoods index, with coordinates and median guide prices
About page explaining the architecture panel and how instructions are vetted
Partner profiles — one contact from first call through to handover
A single property page, leading with the architect and completion year
The journal, carrying market reports and essays on architecture
Full collection view, filtered by neighbourhood
Contact page with the enquiry form and office details

projects.brief: Estate agency websites are organised around filters, floor area and price, which is exactly the language Alvara sells against. Their proposition is authorship: the architect is the product. The site had to read like an architecture publication while still working as a property portal, and had to hold that character across sixteen pages and two themes.
projects.approach: Hand-built rather than assembled from a template, so the typography could carry the editorial weight the positioning needs. Listings lead with the architect and the year the house was completed, with bedroom counts demoted to a supporting line. Photography sits at full width and is never cropped to a uniform card. Light and dark were designed as two finished treatments rather than one inverted into the other.
projects.outcome: A property site that reads as a publication and still performs as a portal. The collection, neighbourhood and journal sections give the agency somewhere to argue a position rather than only list stock, and the architect credit runs consistently from the index through to each individual house.
projects.about:
Alvara House is a boutique estate agency on the Pacific Northwest coast representing architect-designed homes, and the site was built to sell the way the agency actually talks. Every listing credits the architect who drew the house and the year it was completed, treating each property as authored work rather than a set of measurements. The design leans editorial throughout — generous type, full-width photography and a restrained palette — so the site reads closer to an architecture publication than a property portal.

The build runs to sixteen pages: a home page, the full property collection, individual house listings, four service pages, nine neighbourhood guides, partner profiles, a journal with its own article template, careers, an FAQ and the enquiry flow. Each one shares a single type system and grid, so the character holds from the collection index through to a single listing without the layout resetting between sections.

A defining feature is the fully realised dual-theme experience. Light and dark are designed as two finished treatments rather than one inverted into the other, with photography, surface tones and contrast tuned separately in each. Alongside that sit considered scroll and hover motion, a listing architecture that puts authorship above bedroom counts, and an enquiry flow built for a market where buyers ask for drawings rather than brochures.

The result is a property site that reads as a publication and still performs as a portal. The collection, neighbourhood and journal sections give the agency somewhere to argue a position rather than simply list stock, and the architect credit carries consistently from the index through to every individual house.

projects.title: Ines Calder
projects.metaTitle: Ines Calder — Website Design Case Study | Visuvate
projects.overview: Ines Calder is a website for a London business coach who works with founders and CEOs. Clear programmes with fixed fees, a twelve-month method and real client results give a busy CEO enough to decide, and a discovery call form makes the next step easy.
projects.brief: Executive coaching is sold on trust, and most coach websites offer a headshot, a wall of quotes and a contact form. Ines needed a site that lets a busy CEO see how she works, what it costs and what changes for clients in a few minutes, before they ever pick up the phone.
projects.approach: We led with a full-bleed portrait and a one-line promise, then answered doubts in the order a CEO has them: familiar problems, four programmes with fixed monthly fees and a twelve-month method in four phases. A cream page with navy panels and saffron accents keeps it warm and serious.
projects.outcome: The site now does the first meeting’s work: a founder can recognise their problem, see the fees and the shape of a year, read results from client case studies and request a discovery call in minutes. It runs on WordPress with Elementor, so Ines can edit every section herself.
projects.about:
Ines Calder is a complete website for a business coach who works with the founders and CEOs of growing companies in London. It was designed to make the decision easy, with fixed monthly fees, a clear method and results written up as client case studies.

The site includes Home, Coaching with four programmes, Approach, Results with four client case studies, About, a Journal of short articles, Contact, Privacy and Terms pages, with a discovery call form on every path.

The visual direction pairs a cream page with deep navy panels and saffron accents, Host Grotesk headlines with an italic serif for emphasis and a large portrait-led hero. A pinned twelve-month timeline, a results slider and a working-week chart give the page movement without noise.

Built on WordPress with Elementor, almost everything is a native, editable section, with custom elements only for the forms and a few drawn objects, so Ines can change copy, fees and pages herself.

projects.title: Devansh Portfolio
projects.metaTitle: Devansh Portfolio — Website Design Case Study | Visuvate
projects.overview: Devansh Prakash’s portfolio website is a comprehensive showcase of creative expertise across web design, graphic design, video production, and 3D modeling. The site combines modern aesthetics, smooth interactions, and structured presentation for an engaging experience.
projects.brief: A multi-disciplinary creative — web design, graphic design, video, 3D — needed one portfolio that didn’t read as four stapled together. The risk with range is incoherence: the site had to prove versatility while feeling like the work of a single, decided sensibility.
projects.approach: We gave every discipline the same architectural treatment: one grid, one typographic system, one rhythm of reveal — so a 3D render and a brand identity sit side by side as equals. A CMS keeps all four streams publishable, and custom-coded interactions add the layer of craft the work itself promises.
projects.outcome: The portfolio now argues for hiring the person, not just a skill. Visitors can enter through any discipline and leave understanding the whole practice, and the site grows with each new project without diluting its point of view.
projects.about:
The Devansh Prakash portfolio website is a multi-disciplinary showcase built to highlight creativity and versatility across various design domains. Designed and developed from scratch, it embodies a dark, cinematic aesthetic that enhances visual storytelling while maintaining professional clarity.

The site introduces a strong personal brand identity, establishing an immediate sense of expertise and modern craftsmanship. Each section is thoughtfully categorized — from website design and 3D modeling to video production and graphic design — allowing visitors to explore a wide range of projects with seamless navigation and fluid transitions.

Dynamic project grids and subtle motion effects keep the browsing experience intuitive and visually appealing. The layout balances minimal design with impactful typography, ensuring every project stands out while maintaining a cohesive visual rhythm.

Beyond aesthetics, the portfolio serves as a functional demonstration of Devansh’s technical and creative range — from interactive web layouts to product renderings and motion visuals. The site acts not only as a digital portfolio but as an evolving representation of creative progression, strategy, and precision-driven design.

projects.title: Wrenmoor Heath
projects.metaTitle: Wrenmoor Heath — Website Design Case Study | Visuvate
projects.overview: Wrenmoor Heath is a golf club website built around the question every visitor asks first: can I play, and when? A live tee sheet, a hole-by-hole yardage guide and clear membership fees replace the usual brochure.
projects.brief: A private heathland club wanted a website that works as hard as its starter. Visitors need to see weekday availability and green fees at once, prospective members need honest subscriptions and a joining process, and the course itself had to be shown properly rather than as a gallery of stock fairways.
projects.approach: We built the site around the round itself. A full-width hero puts the golfer and the club name together, the homepage carries a working tee sheet, every hole has its own aerial with yardages drawn over it, and membership fees are set out as a simple table. Type is tall and compact, in forest green with one lime accent.
projects.outcome: The site now answers the practical questions in the order golfers ask them: a tee time for a guest, the fees, what the course plays like hole by hole, how to join, and where to lunch afterwards. The course, visitors, membership, academy and clubhouse each have a clear page of their own.
projects.about:
Wrenmoor Heath is a complete website for a private heathland golf club, designed to make a first visit and a first membership enquiry simple. It focuses on availability, honest fees and a proper picture of the course, with booking as the main action on every page.

The site includes Home, the Course with a hole-by-hole guide and scorecard, Visitors with weekday tee-time booking and green fees, Membership with subscriptions and the joining process, the Academy with coaching and lesson prices, the Clubhouse with menus and private dining, and Contact with directions, plus Privacy and Terms pages.

The visual direction is bright and bold: white pages, forest green and a single lime accent, set in Sofia Sans Extra Condensed capitals. The hero sets the club name behind the tree line with the golfer in front of it, every hole has an aerial with its yardages and hazards drawn over it, and square-edged panels replace shadows and rounded pills.

Built as a fast static site in Astro with plain TypeScript, Wrenmoor Heath loads quickly on a phone at the first tee, keeps motion to quiet reveals and respects reduced-motion settings. The tee-time, application and enquiry forms are built in.

projects.title: Ironwood
projects.metaTitle: Ironwood — Website Design Case Study | Visuvate
projects.overview: Ironwood is a premium construction company website designed to showcase exceptional craftsmanship through a refined digital experience. Built with a fully integrated dual-theme interface, the website combines immersive architectural imagery, editorial-inspired layouts, and thoughtful interactions to reflect the company's commitment to quality and precision. Every page is crafted to build trust, highlight completed projects, and guide homeowners through Ironwood's custom home and renovation services with clarity and confidence.
projects.brief: A custom-home builder needed a site that could carry the weight of its craft. Construction websites tend to fall into two traps: stock-photo sameness or a plain gallery that leaves the work to speak into silence. Ironwood needed its projects framed the way the homes themselves are built — deliberately, with nothing accidental on the page.
projects.approach: We built Ironwood in Framer around a warm amber-and-charcoal palette and a confident display face, then let structure do the persuading: full-bleed project photography, a CMS so new builds publish without a designer, and a complete dual theme so the site reads as considered in both light and dark. Custom code covers the details Framer alone would round off.
projects.outcome: The finished site presents a builder that clearly sweats the details — because the site visibly does. Projects are browsable by the qualities buyers actually weigh, every page holds the same standard of finish as the hero, and the studio can grow the portfolio from the CMS without touching the design.
projects.about:
Ironwood is a complete premium residential construction website solution designed to showcase custom homes, luxury renovations, and exceptional craftsmanship through a refined digital experience. The project was built with a strong focus on editorial design, immersive visual storytelling, and structured user flow, creating a platform that reflects the quality, precision, and attention to detail behind every project.

The website includes dedicated pages such as Home, About, Services, Projects, Individual Project Showcase, Process, and Contact, each carefully organized to guide visitors through the company's expertise, completed work, and client journey. Clear navigation, thoughtfully structured content, and strategically placed calls to action help homeowners explore services and confidently take the next step.

A defining feature of the project is its fully integrated dual-theme experience, where both light and dark modes are individually designed to provide a consistent premium aesthetic rather than relying on simple color inversion. Combined with a CMS-powered project portfolio, responsive layouts, subtle animations, and polished micro-interactions, the website delivers an engaging experience while remaining easy to manage and scale as new projects are completed.

The final result is a sophisticated digital platform that strengthens Ironwood's brand identity, showcases its craftsmanship with confidence, and provides prospective clients with a seamless experience that reflects the same level of quality found in every home the company builds.

projects.title: Longitude Society
projects.metaTitle: Longitude Society — Travel Website Case Study | Visuvate
projects.overview: Longitude Society is a private-expedition travel studio designed and built end to end — six pages that run from a full-screen hero into a register of open journeys, an atlas of forty-one countries, the planners behind them and an enquiry form, so the conversation starts on the site itself.
projects.brief: A travel brand that sells bespoke planning has nothing to show but photographs everyone else also has. The site had to make an atelier of eleven planners feel deliberate and rare, without listing packages like a tour operator.
projects.approach: We built six pages around one idea: every journey is drawn, not sold. A full-screen hero, a register of the routes open now, an atlas of forty-one countries, and a timeline showing how seven months actually overlap.
projects.outcome: The site now reads as a studio rather than a catalogue. A visitor can judge the method in a single scroll, see which travel windows are still free, and send an enquiry that already carries the shape of the trip.
projects.about:
Longitude Society is a concept brand for a small atelier of planners who design private journeys to remote places, built to prove that a travel site can sell judgement rather than packages — which is the hardest thing in the category to put on a page.

Six pages carry it: a home that opens on a full-screen frame, an Expeditions register of the routes currently open, an Atlas of forty-one countries with a pin for each, The Atelier for the people and the method, a How it works timeline, and an enquiry page shaped like a travel document.

The site is hand-built in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with its typefaces embedded in the page rather than fetched from a CDN, so it opens as readily on a hotel connection as on a desk.

Interaction is used only where it earns its place: a hero search that composes an enquiry, an atlas that opens a country on hover or keyboard, seven months of planning drawn as overlapping bars, and dispatches from past travellers printed like boarding passes.

projects.title: Meridian eCom
projects.metaTitle: Meridian eCom — Website Design Case Study | Visuvate
projects.overview: Meridian is a premium eCommerce experience for a Swiss watchmaker, presenting mechanical timepieces across men's, women's, sports, and smart collections through a refined, gallery-like shopping flow built for a slower, more considered kind of browsing.
projects.brief: A Swiss watchmaker needed a store that sells the way a boutique does — unhurried, precise, certain of its worth. Most ecommerce templates optimise for volume and noise; mechanical timepieces need the opposite: room, restraint, and product photography treated like the product itself.
projects.approach: We built a gallery-first storefront in Wix Studio: collections for men’s, women’s, sport, and smart lines, each presented on deep neutral grounds with the watch as the only saturated object on screen. Payments, filtering, and category browsing run on the platform’s commerce layer, so the elegance sits on proven checkout plumbing.

The Who We Are section builds credibility by emphasizing the clinic’s long-standing experience and commitment to quality veterinary services. The Our Values and Services sections highlight the clinic’s philosophy and offerings, including vet care, grooming, urgent care, and boarding, through clean iconography and structured layouts.

A well-placed call-to-action area allows users to book appointments or reach out easily, supported by a contact form that simplifies client communication. The footer ties the design together with brand colors, essential links, and social media integration, maintaining a polished and cohesive look.

Developed in Wix Studio, the Guardian Vets website balances accessibility and warmth with professional presentation. It not only strengthens the clinic’s digital identity but also delivers a seamless, trust-driven user experience for both new and returning pet owners.
